Memorandum of Judgment

_______________________________________________________

The Court:

[
1
]

This appeal challenges the rulings of a case
management judge made in response to the appellants’ defiance of court orders
and directions.

Background

[
2
]

This case has a long and very sad history. For
the purpose of this appeal it may be reduced to the following narrative.

[
3
]

The appellants, a married couple, are the
grandparents of three children at the center of a custody/adoption dispute.
Sadly, Mrs. M passed away before this appeal could be heard; only Mr. M is
before us now.

[
4
]

In 2004, the appellants’ son, NM, (the father),
then 24 years old, entered into a relationship with NMF, (the mother), then 16
years old. NMF was soon pregnant with the couple’s first child; two other
children followed.

[
5
]

For a time, the couple and their children lived
in Calgary with the appellants. On May 2, 2012, Director of Child and Family
Services, (the Director), acting on evidence that one of the children had been
sexually abused, apprehended all three. The Director subsequently applied for a
Permanent Guardianship Order (PGO). The children were placed in foster care
pending the determination of that application. Those placements were strictly
confidential: the identity and location of the foster parents were not
disclosed. Still, the appellants were able to locate their grandchildren and talk
to them prior to the PGO hearing, contrary to the instructions of the Director.

[
6
]

On one occasion, the children had to be moved to
a different foster home due to the relentless intrusions of the appellants. That
transfer was also done confidentially but within weeks the appellants were
again able to discover the location of the new foster home.

[
7
]

Remarkably, the appellants were also able to
learn the habits of the foster parents and began showing up when the
grandchildren were engaged in activities outside of the home such as swimming
lessons. In addition, they would phone and email the foster home. On occasion,
the appellants were able to communicate with the grandchildren directly and
whisper to them, encouraging them to recant allegations that their father (NM)
had sexually assaulted one of them. These efforts greatly concerned the
Director who, on September 5, 2013, ordered that the appellants may no longer
have access to the children or communicate with them.

[
8
]

Still, the appellants persisted, on one occasion
even sitting in a van taking photographs of their granddaughter while she was attending
the Calgary Jewish Academy.

[
9
]

The Director’s application for permanent
guardianship of the children was decided following a 20-day hearing. The
appellants and their other son, (GM), had asked to be appointed guardians. The
father, NM, did not; and neither did the mother, NMF, who advised that she was
unable to care for her children.

[
10
]

The father has since been convicted of numerous
offences related to the sexual assault of his daughter and sentenced to 16
years’ imprisonment for those crimes. His appeals to this court  from conviction
and sentence have now been dismissed.

[
11
]

Following the PGO hearing, the presiding judge
issued a comprehensive judgment explaining his decision to award permanent
guardianship of the children to the Director:
2014 ABPC 248
.

[
12
]

The children were then placed with the
respondents, who adopted them in a closed adoption that denied access to the
appellants. This closed adoption precipitated a torrent of litigation initiated
by the appellants, attempting first to have the guardianship order set aside,
then suing a number of people in the Director’s office who had contact with the
file. That flood of litigation was only tempered when the appellant, Mr. M, was
declared a vexatious litigant and his court access restricted:
2017 ABPC 12
.

[
13
]

In this case, as with all closed adoptions, the
identity of the adoptive parents was kept strictly confidential. Still, the
appellants were somehow able to identify and locate the respondents who were
then living in Olds, a town in central Alberta. Although the appellants lived
in Calgary, they began visiting Olds, claiming they went there to see friends
and while there would occasionally “swing by” the respondents’ home.

[
14
]

The appellants then wrote the respondents a
lengthy letter introducing themselves as the Jewish grandparents of the
children who wanted to join in raising them. The letter included the following excerpts:

We have learned a lot about you, and
continue to learn more, about your family, your struggles, your happiness and
sorrows, your achievements, your dedications, your steadfastness and much more.

……..

We need to work together for these
children’s prosperity, cultural-religious mental needs and educational
upbringing. Thus we all need to cooperate and coordinate our mutual
involvements. We perhaps finally can be real grandparents, children’s Sabba and
Nana. We have no intention to remove the children from you by any means,
at
this moment in time
. [Emphasis in original]

And finally:

Do you want to spend lots of time in
courts, spending your wealth on lawyers? There are organizations with deep
pockets who are ready to go after you and get these Jewish children back into
the Jewish fold.
[Emphasis in original]

[
15
]

This latter comment is significant and will be
referred to again.

[
16
]

When that overture went unanswered, the
appellants were able to discover the name and address of the adoptive mother’s
mother and on August 10, 2018 wrote to her, beseeching her to intercede on
their behalf with the respondents.

[
17
]

The respondents then applied to a judge of the
Court of Queen’s Bench for a permanent restraining order and an order
prohibiting the appellants from posting information about them and their adopted
children on social media and requiring the appellants to remove any such
information they had already posted. That order was granted on August 14, 2018.
Of interest, the appellants had been directed by court order two years earlier,
in August of 2016, to stop posting information that their grandchildren had
been in the care of the Director, failing which they would be found in contempt
of court.

[
18
]

Still the appellants persisted. They ignored the
court order and continued to post on social media information about their
grandchildren and that the Director’s office had taken their grandchildren from
them.

[
19
]

The respondents became so concerned that their
adopted children may be abducted by the appellants, they changed their names
and the names of their children and moved away.

[
20
]

On April 12, 2019, the appellants attended
court to address their contempt. On that occasion they were represented by
counsel.

[
21
]

Prior to court, the appellants’ counsel acknowledged
that Mr. M had ignored the court orders and was therefore guilty of contempt and,
together with the respondents’ counsel, agreed to the sanctions that should be
imposed in response. That agreement was then put before the chambers judge,
Justice Dario, as a form of joint submission. The agreement specified that Mr.
M should be sentenced to six weekends in custody and he and Mrs. M be
restrained from harassing or in any way communicating with the respondents and
from posting any information regarding the respondents and their natural and
adopted children on any form of social media. The appellants were also to take
down all of their earlier postings on social media relating to the respondents
and their children, as well as their Go Fund Me account which referred to the
grandchildren by name.

[
22
]

The agreement further specified that in the event
of a breach Mr. M was to be arrested and be brought to court to show cause why
he should not again be found in contempt. Justice Dario imposed the proposed
sanctions and directed Mr. M pay $1,000 in costs.

[
23
]

Notwithstanding the April 12, 2019 finding of
contempt, Mr. M continued to post information about his grandchildren on social
media, recounting that they had been subject to intervention, “abducted”, by
the Director of Child and Family Services. These actions prompted another
contempt hearing on September 6, 2019.

[
24
]

At that hearing Mr. M was self-represented. His
positions were fluid. At the outset he asked the chambers judge to recuse
herself as he had “observed that she was biased” and he “would not have a fair
hearing”. That application was denied.

[
25
]

When confronted with the most recent messages
posted on social media since the April 12 hearing, Mr. M claimed he did not
recognize them although the posts contained his name and at least one was accompanied
by his photograph. He suggested the respondents may have posted them.

[
26
]

Then he argued that these posts did not violate

section 126.2
of the
Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act
, RSA 2000,
c C-12 (the
Act
) because they were posted after the children were no
longer in the care of the government.
Section 126.2(1)
of the
Act
states:

No person shall publish the name or a
photograph of a child or of the child’s parent or guardian in a manner that
reveals that the child is receiving or
has received intervention services.
[Emphasis
added]

[
27
]

The chambers judge read that provision to Mr. M
and reminded him that he had offered that same excuse in 2016 and was told that
the provision applied not only to children who are receiving intervention
services but also to those who had received such service in the past. Mr. M
denied that he had been corrected in 2016 and assured the chambers judge that
he now understood and would not offend that provision in the future.

[
28
]

There followed this exchange:

THE COURT: You made the exact statement to
me when you and [Mrs. M] were before me in 2016. You said we didn’t understand
it before, we understand it now, we will take the postings down.

DM:     No –

THE COURT: You made that commitment to me.
And you did not –

DM:     We never say that, Your Honour.

THE COURT: You did, sir.

And later:

THE COURT: And I have waited, Sir, for you
to comply with that order. I have been very patient. Since 2016 I have taken no
action up until the most recent proceedings where it’s become apparent that you
have completely disregarded the law. You have completely disregarded your
grandchildren’s interests in having their privacy protected. That is why we are
here today [Mr. M].

….

And I will also
state, sir, that indicating that there had been any kind of sexual interference
by their maternal grandfather is also very, very problematic. You’re not
considering your grandchildren’s emotional response to having this posted to
the world, whether it is true or not.

[
29
]

The chambers judge did not accept Mr. M’s
denial. She directed he pay an outstanding fine of $5,000 and gave him two
months to pay it. She cautioned him that if he continued to post forbidden
emails, more fines and incarceration would be the only remaining sanctions.

[
30
]

Of interest,
section 126.2(4)
of the
Act

provides that:

Any person who contravenes subsection (1) is guilty of an
offence and liable to a fine of not more than $10,000 and in default of payment
to imprisonment for a term of not more than 6 months.

Grounds of Appeal

[
31
]

The chambers judge’s rulings on that day are the
subject of this appeal. Although widely cast, the grounds of appeal may be reduced
to the following:

1.

The conduct of the chambers judge gave rise to a
reasonable apprehension of bias.

2.

The evidence relied upon by the chambers judge
to support the finding of contempt was unreliable.

3.

The hearing was procedurally unfair.

1.

Whether the conduct of the chambers judge gave
rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias

[
32
]

Mr. M maintains that the chambers judge, Justice
Dario, exhibited “bias and hostility toward the [M] family since 2015.” He
asserts, incorrectly, that she had been asked numerous times to recuse herself
from the case but refused. In fact, at the April 12, 2019 hearing when Mr. M
was represented by counsel, that counsel made the following request of Justice
Dario:

…We are suggesting that you be seized with
the matter, since you have familiarity with it.

[
33
]

Mr. M also alleges that Justice Dario displayed
stereotypical bias when she “… commented from the bench that the appellant
should get the ‘fine money’ from the ‘Jewish community’ as they were a source
with deep pockets” (Factum of the appellant at para 46). He maintains the situation
was aggravated when Justice Dario had the word “Jewish” deleted from the
transcript of proceedings.

[
34
]

Again, Mr. M has taken liberties with the
evidence and the facts. What Justice Dario did say regarding this matter was:

Well, before the court, the only information
that I have is what is set out in Exhibit D to the affidavit of Mr. S. and that
exhibit contains a letter signed by Mr. M., which states something to the
effect that he has access to a community with deep pockets, and they are
prepared to litigate this matter.…

[
35
]

In making this comment Justice Dario was simply referencing
the letter the appellants had written the respondents, referred to at paragraph
14 above. The reference to “deep pockets” originated with that letter when the
appellants advised the respondents, “there are organizations with deep pockets
who are ready to go after you and get these Jewish children back into the
Jewish fold.” It is that comment that Justice Dario was paraphrasing when she
made the “deep pockets” reference.

[
36
]

As to the claim that Justice Dario had the word
“Jewish” deleted from the transcript, that too is incorrect. The court has
listened to an audio recording of the proceedings that has not been interfered
with, and the word “Jewish” was not used by Justice Dario on that occasion.

[
37
]

To be clear, Mr. M relies on misrepresentations
to support his claim that Justice Dario was biased against him and his family. Our
review of the record indicates there is no basis in fact to support his claim;
it is spurious. The observations of the judge who declared Mr. M a vexatious
litigant in 2017 are apposite:

The grandparents, as well as the children’s
father, have engaged in numerous defamatory allegations against nearly everyone
who does not support them. These irrational statements have included the
following:

•

Accusing the Calgary Jewish Academy of being
anti-Semitic;

•

Accusing the Jewish Family Services of being
anti-Semitic;

•

Accusing the Director of being anti-Semitic;

•

Calling a Child and Family Services worker a
Muslim terrorist;

•

Comparing Child and Family Services to Nazi
Germany, accusing Child and Family Services of “Jew hatred by an Alberta
Government machinery”;

•

Accusing the Director of brainwashing the
children;

•

Accusing the Director of manufacturing evidence
against the father;

•

Referring to the PGO trial as a “Kangaroo
court”;

•

Alleging the children suffer from Stockholm
syndrome; and

•

Alleging the Provincial Court and just about
everyone else is biased against them.

(
2017 ABPC 12
at para
29
)

[
38
]

This ground of appeal is dismissed for want of
any supporting evidence. Rather than being biased against the appellants,
Justice Dario has been extremely lenient. Such sustained, deliberate defiance
of the law and court orders should not have been allowed to go unsanctioned for
so long.

2.

That the evidence relied upon by the chambers
judge was unreliable

[
39
]

Mr. M has been posting information on social
media since at least 2014 alleging that his grandchildren had been “abducted”
by the Director and placed with the respondents who adopted them. Some posts
were accompanied by photographs of the children and even photographs of Mr. M. When
confronted with new posts, he often equivocated between suggesting he didn’t
post them, but if he did, they did not offend the law.

[
40
]

On April 12, 2019, with counsel, he agreed that
he had posted the offending messages on social media and agreed he deserved to
be sanctioned for doing so.

[
41
]

The postings at issue in the September 6 hearing
were generally consistent with the earlier posts and the trial judge accepted
Mr. M was responsible for them. That finding is supported by his conduct
throughout and his position that the posts did not violate
section 126.2

because the children were no longer in the Director’s care. The chambers
judge’s finding on this point is entitled to deference and we can see no basis
to interfere.

3.

Whether the procedure followed by the chambers
judge was unfair

[
42
]

We have reviewed the transcripts of the
September 6 and April 12 hearings and can find no evidence to suggest that the
procedure followed was in any way unfair. To the contrary, we think that from
the beginning the appellants have not only been treated fairly but also with
great leniency. As noted by the chambers judge, they had been violating a court
order and the law since 2016 and were not sanctioned until April 12, 2019. And,
even then, the chambers judge was reluctant to impose the $5,000 fine as Mr. M
insisted he was an impecunious senior, unable to pay it. She responded by
giving him two months to produce evidence of his impecuniosity so that she
might consider reducing the fine. No such evidence was forthcoming.

[
43
]

The appeal is dismissed.

Costs

[
44
]

As to costs, the respondents are awarded costs
of $5,000.

[
45
]

A final observation. The court has some difficulty
understanding why the respondents have been left to prosecute these persistent
breaches of the
Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act
.
To clarify, the
contempt on this occasion consisted of Mr. M violating section 126.2 of the
Act

and court orders directing him to stop doing so. We acknowledge the restraining
order also directed he have no contact with the respondents, but his contempt focussed
on his continued violation of
section 126.2
of the
Act.
It concerns us
that enforcing this provincial legislation somehow became the respondents’
responsibility and financial burden.

Appeal heard on April
6, 2021

Calgary,
Alberta

this
30th day of July, 2021
